name: Roman Republic

areaKm2.note: Peninsular Italy south of the Arno-Rubicon line ~130,000 km2 (the low bound Seshat codes for 264 BCE, https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/183) + Sicily outside Hiero's kingdom ~20,000 + Sardinia 24,100 and Corsica 8,700 (modern island areas) = ~183,000; high adds the ager Gallicus and the Cisalpine land conquered in 225-222. The historical-basemaps world_bc300 polygon (37,893 km2, Latium and Campania only) badly understates the 218 extent and is used for the map only.

population.note: Seshat codes the Middle Republic at 3.5-4.0 million for 264-133 BCE (low). De Ligt (Peasants, Citizens and Soldiers, 2012, as reviewed at https://bmcr.brynmawr.edu/?p=37690) reads the Polybian manpower list of 225 (Polybius 2.24, https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/2*.html) as 4.2 million for Italy; Brunt (isbn:0198142838, ch. 5) has ~3 million free in peninsular Italy plus slaves. Added: the provinces of Sicily (outside Hiero's kingdom) and Sardinia-Corsica, ~0.3-0.6 million (educated guess). Covers Rome, the Latin colonies and the Italian allies south of the Apennines; Cisalpine Gaul (in revolt in 218) and Syracuse are not counted.

urbanization.note: Educated guess. Seshat (https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/183) codes Rome at 210,000 in 200 BCE; Capua, Tarentum, Neapolis, Syracuse (outside) and the Latin colonies were the other towns of 5,000+. ~0.5 million urban of ~4.5 million.

activePersonnel.note: Field armies of 218 (70,200 per Livy 21.17) + fleet crews (supportPersonnel, ~66,000) + garrisons in Sicily, Sardinia and Tarentum (0-15,000, estimate; Polybius 2.24.13 records two legions of 4,200 in Sicily and Tarentum in 225). Livy 21.17 (https://archive.org/stream/livybook2125seco00livy/livybook2125seco00livy_djvu.txt): six legions voted for 218, 24,000 Roman infantry and 1,800 cavalry, 40,000 allied infantry and 4,400 allied cavalry; Sempronius 2 legions + 16,000 allied foot + 1,800 allied horse, Scipio 2 legions + 14,000 + 1,600, the praetor Manlius in Gaul 2 legions + 10,000 allied foot + 1,000 allied and 600 Roman horse. Brunt, Italian Manpower (isbn:0198142838, Appendix 26, legions by year) and Lazenby (isbn:0806130040, ch. 3) accept six legions for 218. Convention: the six legions and allied contingents levied for 218 are under arms at the snapshot date and counted as active; men on the census rolls who must still be levied are in trainedReserves. audit 2026-10-30: grade B -> C: rests on an ancient chronicler's figure (SOURCES.md: at most C), accepted by modern historians.

trainedReserves.note: Polybius 2.24 lists 250,000 Roman and Campanian foot and 23,000 horse and ~450,000 allied men on the rolls of 225 (ancient figures; Brunt, isbn:0198142838, ch. 4, accepts their order of magnitude). Many had served in the Gallic war of 225-222. Callable within ~30 days: Rome raised 8 legions for Cannae (216); range is an estimate of men already trained.

supportPersonnel.note: 220 quinqueremes (Livy 21.17, https://archive.org/stream/livybook2125seco00livy/livybook2125seco00livy_djvu.txt; Polybius 3.41.2, https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/3*.html: 160 + 60 ships) x 300 rowers (Polybius 1.26.7, https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/1*.html) = 66,000 oarsmen (socii navales, mostly from the Greek allies) + 20 light galleys. Marines were legionaries and are counted in the legions. Low assumes not all hulls crewed in spring; high adds staff and engineers. audit 2026-10-30: grade B -> C: rests on an ancient chronicler's figure (SOURCES.md: at most C), accepted by modern historians.

mobilizationRatio.note: Brunt (isbn:0198142838, ch. 22 and Appendix 26) counts ~22-25 legions (~100,000-120,000 citizens) plus at least as many allies under arms in 214-211, ~6-7% of the population before fleet crews. Polybius 2.24.16 (https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/2*.html) claims more than 700,000 foot and 70,000 horse able to bear arms in 225 (~16% of a 4.5 million population), an upper bound.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Hastati, principes and triarii: 3,000 of each legion's 4,000-4,200 foot and ~80% of the allied foot (18,000 Roman + 32,000 allied = 50,000) + garrisons (high). Livy 21.17 (https://archive.org/stream/livybook2125seco00livy/livybook2125seco00livy_djvu.txt): six legions voted for 218, 24,000 Roman infantry and 1,800 cavalry, 40,000 allied infantry and 4,400 allied cavalry; Sempronius 2 legions + 16,000 allied foot + 1,800 allied horse, Scipio 2 legions + 14,000 + 1,600, the praetor Manlius in Gaul 2 legions + 10,000 allied foot + 1,000 allied and 600 Roman horse. Brunt, Italian Manpower (isbn:0198142838, Appendix 26, legions by year) and Lazenby (isbn:0806130040, ch. 3) accept six legions for 218. audit 2026-10-30: grade B -> C: rests on an ancient chronicler's figure (SOURCES.md: at most C), accepted by modern historians.

quality.note: Rubric 0.75-1.0: large scutum, pilum, gladius hispaniensis, bronze pectoral or mail for the wealthier; among the era's best but below the Imperial kit of 100 CE.

training.note: Rubric 0.5: annually levied citizen-soldiers with prior campaign experience (Gallic war 225-222, Illyria 219), not long-service professionals; the legions of 218 were newly enrolled.

count.note: Velites: 1,000-1,200 per legion (6,000) + ~20% of the 40,000 allied foot (8,000, estimate); high adds garrison light troops. Livy 21.17 (https://archive.org/stream/livybook2125seco00livy/livybook2125seco00livy_djvu.txt): six legions voted for 218, 24,000 Roman infantry and 1,800 cavalry, 40,000 allied infantry and 4,400 allied cavalry; Sempronius 2 legions + 16,000 allied foot + 1,800 allied horse, Scipio 2 legions + 14,000 + 1,600, the praetor Manlius in Gaul 2 legions + 10,000 allied foot + 1,000 allied and 600 Roman horse. quality.note: Rubric 0.5: javelins and a small shield.

training.note: Rubric 0.25-0.5: the youngest and poorest citizens.

count.note: Roman citizen cavalry 1,800 + allied cavalry 4,400 (Livy 21.17) = 6,200; high adds garrison horse. Roman cavalry fought as close-order shock horse. Livy 21.17 (https://archive.org/stream/livybook2125seco00livy/livybook2125seco00livy_djvu.txt): six legions voted for 218, 24,000 Roman infantry and 1,800 cavalry, 40,000 allied infantry and 4,400 allied cavalry; Sempronius 2 legions + 16,000 allied foot + 1,800 allied horse, Scipio 2 legions + 14,000 + 1,600, the praetor Manlius in Gaul 2 legions + 10,000 allied foot + 1,000 allied and 600 Roman horse. quality.note: Rubric 0.5: era-typical; outclassed by Hannibal's Spanish and Numidian horse at the Ticinus and Trebia.

training.note: Rubric 0.5: wealthy citizens with private riding experience, little unit training.

count.note: Livy 21.17: 220 quinqueremes launched for 218 (160 to Sempronius, 60 to Scipio), matching Polybius 3.41.2 (https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/3*.html). Lazenby (isbn:0806130040, ch. 3) accepts the figure; low allows hulls not yet manned. audit 2026-10-30: grade B -> C: rests on an ancient chronicler's figure (SOURCES.md: at most C), accepted by modern historians.

quality.note: Rubric 0.75: quinqueremes built on the Punic model, unchallenged at sea after 241.

training.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: experienced allied Greek oarsmen, Roman admirals were annual magistrates.

count.note: Livy 21.17: 20 light galleys (celoces), 12 of them with Sempronius; high adds allied patrol craft. audit 2026-10-30: grade B -> C: rests on an ancient chronicler's figure (SOURCES.md: at most C), accepted by modern historians.

commandQuality.note: Rubric 0.5: competent tribunes and centurions, but command rotated among annually elected consuls (Sempronius at the Trebia, Flaminius at Trasimene) with no staff system.

cohesion.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: citizen militia with strong civic and manipular identity; the Latin and Italian allies stayed largely loyal until Cannae.

morale.note: Rubric 0.75: motivated, recent victories (First Punic War, Gallic war 225-222, Illyria 219); war declared over Saguntum.

weapons.note: Anchor 3 (iron weapons, torsion artillery) plus pilum and gladius hispaniensis; below the Imperial 3.3.

armor.note: Anchor 3: bronze pectoral for most, mail for the wealthy (Polybius 6.23).

fortification.note: Anchor 3: ashlar city walls (Servian wall), fortified Latin colonies, fortified marching camps.

logistics.note: Anchor 3: engineered roads (Via Appia 312, Via Aurelia 241, Via Flaminia 220) and allied grain contributions.

communications.note: Between anchors 2 and 3: couriers on the consular roads; no relay-post system yet.

isr.note: Year anchor 3 at the low end: cavalry scouting was weak (Trebia, Trasimene ambushes).

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project 2023 via https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-maddison-project-database.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true: Italy year 1 CE = 1,407 (2011 int$). Third-century Italy was poorer, less urban and less monetised than Augustan Italy; scaled to ~0.6-0.9 of the 1 CE value, mid 1,000 (close to Greece 1,275 and Tunisia 1,116 for 1 CE).

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess: unpaid-in-kind citizen service with a modest stipendium, the tributum levied in war; low is the peacetime level, high the 214-211 war effort.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess: overwhelmingly agrarian; crafts in Capua, Etruria and the Greek cities.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess: self-sufficient in grain with Sicilian and Sardinian tithes as a surplus; Polybius 2.24 notes large stockpiles in 225.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in an ancient Greek-type age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model used for all classical and medieval snapshots.

roadKm.note: Educated guess: Via Appia (Rome-Capua-Beneventum-Venusia), Via Latina, Valeria, Aurelia, Flaminia (Rome-Ariminum ~330 km) and Salaria; ~2,000 km of engineered road.

majorPorts.note: Ostia, Neapolis, Puteoli, Tarentum, Brundisium, Pisa, Lilybaeum, Panormus, Caralis (fleet-capable ports, estimate).

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess: Campanian, Etruscan and South Italian Greek coasting trade; Rome itself was not yet a major trading power.

supplyRangeKm.note: By analogy with Engels (isbn:0520042727, ch. 1): pre-modern armies could operate ~1-2 weeks' march from a depot or the sea.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess: ~0.07-0.11 oxen, mules, donkeys and horses per inhabitant x population.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.2: familiar terrain and local supply plus a network of fortified Latin colonies and allied cities that largely held after Cannae.

notes: Snapshot = spring 218 BCE, the outbreak of the Second Punic War; forces are the six legions and allied contingents voted for 218 (Livy 21.17) and the 220-quinquereme fleet. Population convention: Rome, the Latin colonies and the Italian allies (socii) south of the Apennines, plus the provinces of Sicily and Sardinia-Corsica; Hiero's Syracuse (an ally), Massalia and Cisalpine Gaul are not counted (includes = []). Polybius 2.24's manpower list of 225 (700,000 foot and 70,000 horse able to bear arms) is used only for reserves; the population debate (Brunt's low count vs high counts) is reflected in the range. Border uses historical-basemaps world_bc300 (nearest file at or before 218), whose Roman Republic polygon shows only Latium and Campania (37,893 km2): the map polygon understates the 218 extent by about a factor of five; areaKm2 is researched separately. audit 2026-10-30: border left at hb:bc300:Roman Republic (37,893 km2, Latium and Campania): the nearer hb:bc200:Rome (~518,000 km2) adds eastern Spain, Cisalpine Gaul and the Po valley, Carthaginian or Gallic in 218, so it is not better; neither matches the ~190,000 km2 area.
